text:
This section examines Main-film conclusion
(3–4 minutes) from first

principles. Keep two questions separate:
does changing the order change

the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method beat

a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? Return to

the six instruction cards from the cold
open. Summarize: order

can create large performance variation
even when components do not

change; mutation, representation, and
replacement must match the landscape;

convergence in the limit does not
guarantee budget-efficient search; exact

enumeration and random baselines exposed
both successes and boundaries;

transferable position effects may be more
valuable than a single

best ordering; prism’s mature contribution
is the

measure–diagnose–select–verify protocol.
End on the paper’s refined

question: > “Before searching for the best
order, determine whether

order matters, whether the landscape is
searchable, and whether a

cheaper landscape can guide the expensive
one.” The distinction is

part of the result. A large ordering
effect does not

automatically imply an evolutionary-search
advantage, and almost-sure

convergence does not promise practical
efficiency.
